newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japan face dilemma - what to do about yen?.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan face dilemma - what to do about yen?.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The United States and Japan face a dilemma over currencies -- they both believe the dollar may have risen too far against the yen but admit they could have a hard time convincing traders in financial markets of that.
With U.S. interest rates high and possibly rising and Japanese interest rates low, U.S. and Japanese officials admit that investors are more prone to buy dollars than sell them.

"It's difficult to argue that the dollar is not consistent with fundamentals when U.S. interest rates are rising," said one official from the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations, who declined to be named.

But that is exactly what Washington and Tokyo are trying to do. They fear the strength of the dollar against the yen may be setting the stage for a ballooning of Japan's trade surplus by making Japanese products more competitive.

"We share the concern expressed by the Japanese authorities ... about recent movements in the yen because of the impact on Japan's external surplus," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said earlier this month.

G7 officials said some of that heightened concern could be echoed by finance ministers and central bankers from the group after their meeting Sunday. "I assume some of that will show through," one said.

But it is not clear how far the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- will go. One Japanese official said it may be difficult for the group to go beyond its last currency statement in Berlin.
At its last meeting, the group signalled its desire for stable currency rates by saying the dollar's steep fall of two years earlier had been corrected.
"There are suspicions that misalignments are developing, particularly on dollar-yen, although they are not tremendous," one G7 official said.

Japanese officials have been the most vociferous among the G7 in voicing their concern about the current pattern of currency rates, even going so far as to hint at dollar-selling intervention to bring the greenback down.
European officials, by contrast, have been more relaxed, although Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer did say last week that the German central bank did not want a weak mark.
One G7 official put it this way. The dollar looks neutral against the mark, neither too high nor too low. But against the yen, its looks "asymmetric" -- that is, too high.
But it is a stretch from the G7 making that judgment to deciding to step in to sell dollars for yen.

On its face, dollar sales by the Federal Reserve while it is tightening credit appears contradictory, one G7 official said. In seeking to push down the dollar, the Fed would be putting upward pressure on import prices when it is trying to contain inflation.
But that has not stopped the Fed in the past from pursuing such a strategy when it felt both the dollar and inflation were too high.
That policy, though, carried a price -- the Fed arguably then had to raise interest rates more than otherwise to offset the inflationary impact of a weaker dollar.

In their effort to keep the dollar in check, Japanese officials have taken to warning recently that record-low interest rates in Japan could rise. That would make the yen a more lucrative currency for investors to hold.
But given the uncertain outlook for the Japanese economy, several G7 officials said they do not see the Bank of Japan raising rates anytime soon.
"I don't think there is any risk that interest rates will go up in the next three months or even the next six months," one G7 official said.
